title: Ecclesiastes 12:1–8
context: The Preacher calls the young to remember their Creator before the evil days come. A sequence of images follows, and readers have understood it in several ways: as an allegory of the aging body, as a picture of a gathering storm, as a great household falling into decline, or as a funeral scene, with some combining these readings. The silver cord, golden bowl, pitcher, and wheel are commonly read as images of death. The dust returns to the earth, the spirit returns to God, and the poem closes with the refrain that opened the book.

verses.text: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw near, when you will say, “I have no pleasure in them;”
verses.arminianNotes: Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come. Arminian readers see an urgent call to turn to God while the heart is still responsive and life is full of strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see remembering as more than recalling: it means living in awareness of God as Creator. The call grounds the whole poem that follows in the relationship between creature and Maker.

verses.text: Before the sun, the light, the moon, and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain;
verses.arminianNotes: Before the sun, moon, and stars are darkened and the clouds return after the rain. Arminian readers note that some read this as dimming sight or failing faculties, others as an approaching storm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image of clouds returning after rain suggests troubles that no longer pass quickly. Whether read as aging or as a storm, the picture is of light fading.

verses.text: in the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look out of the windows are darkened,
verses.arminianNotes: The keepers tremble, the strong men bow, the grinders cease, and those at the windows grow dark. Arminian readers note the common reading of trembling hands, bent legs, lost teeth, and dimming eyes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that others read the verse as a great house in decline, with servants weakened and few left to work. The notes offer both readings without choosing one.

verses.text: and the doors shall be shut in the street; when the sound of the grinding is low, and one shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of music shall be brought low;
verses.arminianNotes: The doors are shut, the grinding is low, one rises at a bird’s voice, and the daughters of music are brought low. Arminian readers note readings of failing hearing and light, restless sleep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the household reading sees a quiet, shuttered home, its daily work fading. The allegorical and literal readings both convey diminishing life.

verses.text: yes, they shall be afraid of heights, and terrors will be on the way; and the almond tree shall blossom, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail; because man goes to his everlasting home, and the mourners go about the streets;
verses.arminianNotes: Fear of heights, terrors on the way, the almond blossoms, the grasshopper drags, and desire fails as man goes to his everlasting home. Arminian readers note readings of white hair and failing strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the mourners in the streets suggest a funeral scene, and many interpreters read this verse as the approach of death. The exact meaning of some images is debated.

verses.text: before the silver cord is severed, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is broken at the spring, or the wheel broken at the cistern,
verses.arminianNotes: Before the silver cord is severed, the golden bowl broken, the pitcher broken at the spring, or the wheel at the cistern. Arminian readers see images of life’s precious vessel shattered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many read the cord and bowl as a hanging lamp whose light goes out, and the pitcher and wheel as a well that can no longer draw water. Each image commonly signals death.

verses.text: and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
verses.arminianNotes: The dust returns to the earth, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Arminian readers hear Genesis 3:19 and Genesis 2:7, the creation of man from dust and the breath of life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ecclesiastes 3:21 earlier asked who knows whether the spirit goes upward. This verse affirms that the spirit returns to God; the two passages are named without harmonizing.

verses.text: “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher. “All is vanity!”
verses.arminianNotes: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, all is vanity. Arminian readers see the refrain that opened the book (1:2) now closing the poem, framing the whole search under the sun.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this frame around the book as summing up the Preacher’s observation of life’s fleeting nature. As in 1:2, vanity may suggest vapor, breath, or what is fleeting, insubstantial, enigmatic, or even absurd; the sense may shift with context.
